title: Executive Order Ninety-066 and Japanese Internment
description: An examination of Executive Order Ninety-066, detailing the forced removal and incarceration of Japanese Americans during World War II, camp conditions, and subsequent legislative redress decades later.
why_us: Explores a critical chapter of US dark history using authentic archival photographs and records from the National Archives to explain the implementation and consequences of Executive Order 9066.
timely_basis: Maintains an evergreen educational focus on civil liberties, constitutional rights, and historical accountability.

scenes.narration: Following the attack on Pearl Harbor, President Franklin Roosevelt issued Executive Order Ninety-066 in February 1942, authorizing military commanders to remove individuals.
Families faced immense pressure and short notice to liquidate property and abandon homes before being sent to assembly centers.

diagram.title: Evacuation Process Steps
diagram.note: Families received brief notice to arrange affairs before removal.

scenes.narration: Residents lined up outside civil control stations with stacked baggage, awaiting transport to remote inland facilities.
Over one hundred thousand men, women, and children were confined in isolated relocation centers surrounded by barbed wire and guards.
Internees navigated harsh desert weather and barracks life while striving to establish schools and community routines.
Decades later, archival research and the commission examined the policy, evaluating impacts.

diagram.title: Official Review Impact
diagram.note: Investigations led to government acknowledgement and redress.

scenes.narration: Federal legislation provided a formal apology and partial financial restitution to surviving individuals who had been incarcerated.
